webpage.text:
Nine killed in mid-air crash over New York | New York

Nine people were killed today after a sightseeing helicopter carrying Italian tourists collided in mid-air with a small plane near New York and crashed into the Hudson river.

Eyewitnesses saw a wing come off the plane during the collision just after noon US time and watched as the helicopter "fell like a stone" into the river.

Five Italian tourists and the pilot were aboard the helicopter; in the plane, along with the pilot, there were two passengers, one of whom was a child. Another pilot on the ground at the heliport saw the plane approaching and tried to radio an alert to the helicopter above. But the warning was either not heard, or failed to get through in time.

The collision took place just south of the stretch of river where a US Airways jet that had run into trouble after apparently hitting a flock of geese was ditched in January by its pilot, who was hailed as a hero for saving the lives of all 150 people on board.

Two bodies were recovered but there was no hope of finding survivors, said New York's mayor, Michael Bloomberg, who described the incident as "not survivable".

He said that police had found one piece of wreckage in the murky waters of the Hudson and that the search would probably continue for a few days.

"This has changed from a rescue to a recovery mission. There's not going to be a happy ending," he added.

The plane, which was a single-engine Piper PA-32R-300, had taken off earlier from Teterboro Airport in New Jersey and was flying south along the river when it appeared to lose control as it banked steeply and struck the helicopter close to the shore line of Hoboken, New Jersey.

The helicopter, operated by Liberty Helicopter, the largest sightseeing and charter helicopter operator in the north-east US, had taken off moments earlier from West 30th Street in Manhattan.

Hundreds of people on both sides of the mile-wide river watched as the two aircraft appeared to break apart, with the rotary blades detaching from the helicopter, opposite the west side of Manhattan.

On the waterfront at Hoboken, people scattered as pieces of the debris fell from the sky while a wheel from one of the aircraft lay on Hoboken's Sinatra Drive.

"I saw the plane coming down and the helicopter coming across," said Hilda Igartua, 53, of Union City, New Jersey, who added that the plane's trajectory did not change after the collision but the helicopter came apart and spun down in pieces.

"We saw the helicopter propellers fly all over," said Katie Tanski, of Hoboken.

Melissa Green, 33, and her husband were in a park along the river on the New York side and heard the crash. "We turned around and saw these two mushroom splashes," Green said.

"What was really weird is there was no wreckage, nothing. I hope they find the people, but I don't know. They just disappeared," she explained.

"First I saw a piece of something flying through the air. Then I saw the helicopter going down into the water," she said, adding that the crowd in the park seemed too stunned to react. "I thought it was my imagination."

The weather at the time of the collision was clear and mild. Vessels including water taxis diverted to the scene of the accident along with fire boats and Coast Guard rescue teams but both of the aircraft sank quickly under a strong current.

Police divers were carrying out a search of the river as an investigation was launched by the Federal Aviation Administration.

The accident happened in a busy general aviation corridor over the river that is often filled with sightseeing craft on sunny days.

Pilots have some freedom to pick their own route, as long as they stay under 300m and do not stray too close to Manhattan's skyscrapers.

Accidents are not frequent, but happen every few years. Cory Lidle, a pitcher for the New York Yankees baseball team, and his flight instructor died in 2006 when their plane hit a skyscraper while flying along a popular sightseeing route.

Two years ago, a Liberty helicopter fell 150m to the ground during another sightseeing trip. The pilot was credited with safely landing the aircraft in the Hudson and helping evacuate the seven passengers.

In 1997, a rotor on one of its sightseeing helicopters clipped a Manhattan building, forcing an emergency landing. No one was hurt.

OTD in 2009, N71MC a Piper PA-32R collides with N401LH a Eurocopter AS350 that was on a tour over the Hudson River in New York. All three occupants of the Piper and the 6 occupants of the Eurocopter are killed.  

“The final report by the NTSB concluded that the two primary causes of the accident: (1) the "inherent limitations" of the see-and-avoid concept, which meant that from the airplane pilot's point of view, the helicopter would have appeared as a small, stationary object against a backdrop of the New York City skyline until the final seconds before the collision; and (2) the Teterboro controller's personal phone call, which distracted him from his air traffic control duties and prevented him from correcting the airplane pilot's incorrect readback of the Newark control tower's radio frequency.” - https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/AAR1005.pdf 

https://asn.flightsafety.org/wikibase/67818 

Credit of the two first photos go to Paul Kanagie and Kim Vanvik (https://www.jetphotos.com/photo/6541858).

Manhattan, NY – Passengers Killed In Plane Collision Were Wealthy Jewish Philanthropist

Manhattan, NY – It was a perfect summer day when Steven Altman set out from a suburban airstrip in his single-engine plane, heading up to northern New Jersey to pick up his brother and nephew and take them to the beach.

Join our WhatsApp group

Subscribe to our Daily Roundup Email

There was nothing in the weather forecast or in Altman’s aviation files to portend the horrifying accident that would happen Saturday 1,100 feet over the Hudson River, when his aircraft smashed into a tourist helicopter, killing nine people.

Altman had a clean record and was instrument-rated, meaning he was trained to fly in poor weather if necessary, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. His medical clearance was up to date, the only restriction being he needed glasses for nearsightedness.

“He was perfectly legal and qualified to fly that aircraft,” FAA spokesman Jim Peters said Monday.

FAA records show that Altman, 60, of Ambler, Pa., got a license to fly in 1998, but it was not immediately clear how many hours he had logged. Pilots keep track of their own flight hours, and officials have not yet found Altman’s log book, said Peter Knudson, a spokesman for the National Transportation Safety Board, which is investigating.

The plane, a Piper manufactured in 1976, also had a clean record, according to FAA records. Altman bought it about a decade ago, said Michael V. Chiodo, of Blue Bell, Pa., who sold it to the pilot.

After leaving Pennsylvania, Altman made a stop at the airport in Teterboro, N.J., before flying on with his brother, Daniel, and Daniel’s teenage son, Douglas, on the 114-mile flight to the beach town of Ocean City, N.J.

The trio had just taken off and were flying over the Hudson when the plane crashed into a helicopter carrying a pilot and five Italian tourists. All nine people died.

The Altmans’ immediate family has been reclusive since the accident, but the name is well known in Pennsylvania real estate circles.

Steven Altman owned Altman Management Co., which oversaw more than 14,000 apartments in Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey, according to the company Web site. It was part of The Altman Group of real estate companies, begun by his father in 1949.

Bruce Toll, co-founder of luxury homebuilder Toll Brothers, said the Altman family is well regarded in the building industry and active in local Jewish charities. According to KYW Radio the Altman’s were also involved with their synagogue.

“They’re just thought of as good, honest businessmen,” Toll said Monday, calling the accident tragic.

Gov. Ed Rendell, the former mayor of Philadelphia, said through spokesman Michael Smith on Monday that the Altmans “were an important part of the city’s redevelopment and growth.”

Steven Altman was a member of the Board of Overseers of Albert Einstein Healthcare Network in Philadelphia last year. He was a past president and active member of the Apartment Association of Greater Philadelphia and traveled to Harrisburg in March to meet with lawmakers on related issues.

His profile on the social networking site Linked In says he attended Cornell University. Altman was one of five children, according to a biography of his father, David, posted on the Web site for Angel Flight East.

The agency, which uses volunteer pilots to fly seriously ill patients to medical facilities, is based at Wings, the tiny airfield in Blue Bell where Steven Altman took off before flying to Teterboro.

David Altman, 87, has flown for Angel Flight East since 1993, and Steven Altman traveled as a co-pilot on some missions, agency executive director Maureen Schmidt said Monday.

“They’re just a wonderful family … very generous,” Schmidt said.

The airfield is just a few miles from Steven Altman’s home in Ambler, an affluent suburb about 15 miles north of Philadelphia. Police have prevented reporters from entering the private cul-de-sac where he lived with his wife.

webpage.text:
Helicopter, small plane collide, crash in Hudson River; Mayor Bloomberg: All 9 onboard presumed dead – New York Daily News

Nine people were killed on Saturday after a spectacular midair crash sent a low-flying plane and a tourist helicopter spiraling from a clear blue sky into the Hudson River.

The dead included five Italian tourists just seconds into a sight-seeing tour above the city, both pilots and two passengers on the small single-engine plane – including a 15-year-old. Three bodies were recovered.

“Sadly, it appears to us at this point that this was probably not survivable,” said a somber Mayor Bloomberg. “This is not going to have a happy ending.”

Hundreds watched in disbelief on a sun-splashed summer afternoon as the Piper PA-32 lost a wing and the helicopter shed its still-spinning rotor blades after the mystifying crash.

The witnesses included another chopper pilot at the W. 30th St. helipad, who desperately tried to radio a warning in the seconds before the fatal impact.

“He radioed the accident helicopter and told him, ‘One-lima-hotel, you have a fixed wing behind you,'” National Transportation Safety Board Chairman Deborah Hersman said. “There was no response.”

The pilot watched helplessly as the plane’s right wing slammed into the chopper from behind, raining metal on the river.

“I saw the chopper hit the water like it was a toy,” said Dionis Hernandez, 23, of Brooklyn. “The plane kept flying a little bit. It fell, not too far.”

Hernandez and Amy Molewsky, a 21-year-old NYU student, were standing on Pier 52 when they spotted the low-flying plane approaching the helicopter shortly after noon.

“I thought it was impossible they could crash,” Molewsky said. “And then they actually did. The plane kept flying, the helicopter went straight down.”

Other witnesses on both sides of the river described the plane clipping the rotors of the rising helicopter north of the Statue of Liberty. There was a puff of white smoke, a sound like firecrackers, and then an eerie silence.

“The helicopter was suspended in midair for several seconds before it fell into the water,” recalled Deena Glanzberg, who was visiting Manhattan from Miami. “It wasn’t a head-on. It was a clip.”

The five Italian tourists were on a sight-seeing trip run by Liberty Helicopters, flying in a Eurocopter AS 350. A second helicopter, carrying other members of the Italian tourist group, left around the same time as the doomed flight and returned safely, a police source said.

Tourist Paola Casali, 32, of Rome, saw the four Italians from the second chopper keeping a grim heliport vigil with hollow hopes of a happy reunion.

“They looked very sad,” she said. “They weren’t crying. They were worried.”

The Italian news agency ANSA identified the copter victims as Tiziana Pedrone, Fabio Gallazzi, Giacomo Gallazzi, Michele Norelli and Filippo Norelli. Their family ties were unclear.

Daniel Altman and his son, Doug, 15, were passengers in the plane, which was piloted by his brother Steven, police sources and family said.

The plane had a 30-minute stopover at Teterboro Airport to pick up a passenger, said Hersman. The trio departed at 11:54 a.m., with Altman banking the plane south on a trip scheduled to end in Ocean City, N.J.

Six minutes later, the tower at Newark Airport reported losing contact with the small plane over the Hudson. The single-engine craft, built in 1976, was registered to Altman’s Pennsylvania company.

Wreckage from both aircraft was discovered about 300 yards apart in the waters off New Jersey opposite W. 14th St., Bloomberg said.

The bodies of two Italians were recovered from the wreckage by NYPD scuba divers, while young Doug Altman‘s body was discovered floating in the Hudson, police sources said.

Before calling off the search last night, divers located a third Italian victim stuck in the underwater wreckage – and left a buoy tied to the victim’s leg as a marker for today’s effort, a police source said.

Recovery was hampered by the strong currents and spilled fuel oil that reduced visibility to 2 feet in the already murky, 30-foot deep river.

The crash was the city’s worst air disaster since American Airlines Flight 587 fell from the sky in November 2001, killing 265 people.

“This is a difficult day for all of us at Liberty Helicopters,” a statement from the company said.

The NTSB was conducting an investigation into the deadly crash, and Bloomberg said it was too early to determine who was to blame.

Police sources said the plane pilot, flying south down the river corridor, was likely at fault.

The busy flight corridor, which draws heavy traffic in nice weather, allows pilots to pick their own flight routes if they stay below 1,100 feet. Aircraft are not required to be on the same radio frequency along the route, the mayor said.

A flotilla of rescuers flooded the Hudson within minutes of the crash. Coast Guard ships, police divers and random boaters joined with helicopters in the desperate but ultimately fruitless hunt for survivors. NYPD divers were in the water within seven minutes.

Among the first on the scene was Mark Sedaca, 26, a Chelsea Piers worker who took a 20-foot boat out to the crash scene.

Sedaca said his hopes for another Miracle on the Hudson were quickly dashed. “I just saw debris floating on the water,” he said.

The bulk of the one-winged plane and helicopter sank to the bottom of the Hudson within seconds of the crash, but debris from the chopper and the plane scattered along the Hoboken waterfront, with a wheel landing on Frank Sinatra Drive.

resultats_lens.texte_contexte: Neuf personnes ont été tuées dans une collision en plein vol au-dessus du fleuve Hudson à New York, impliquant un avion Piper PA-32 et un hélicoptère touristique Eurocopter AS 350 exploité par Liberty Helicopters. Les victimes comprennent cinq touristes italiens, les deux pilotes et deux passagers de l'avion, dont un adolescent de 15 ans nommé Doug Altman, voyageant avec son père Daniel Altman et piloté par Steven Altman. Le maire Michael Bloomberg a confirmé qu'il n'y avait probablement pas de survivants. Des témoins ont assisté à la scène depuis des quais à Manhattan.
